title: Paul’s 2026 Bespoked Dresden Reflection – Paul Kalifatidi & Stefan Haehnel
content:
For our final piece of The Radavist’s 2026 Bespoked Dresden coverage, we’re handing the mic over to first-time attendee Paul Kalifatidi. Accompanying Paul’s first impressions and a selection of his photos are exquisite Bespoked booth photos by German photographer Stefan Haehnel. Read on for Paul’s musings and Stefan’s visual artistry…

I went to Bespoked with few expectations; those few being: is an event at the airport going to feel weird? And will there be a noticeable difference between this event and the only other bike show I’ve attended? I was pleasantly surprised by the answer to both.

Bespoked Dresden was held in the international airport, Flughafen Dresden, for the fourth year in a row. For me, it was fresh, as I had never been. The only other bike show, at least one that compared in scope to Bespoked, that I have been to has been the four years of the Made Bike Show in Portland, OR. The two venues could not have been starker in contrast.

This piece wasn’t meant to read like a comparison of the two events; it’s just that these are the only two comparable events I have been to.

Venue Differences

Made was held at Zidell Yards, a largely abandoned boatyard that the city has condemned. The floor is dirty, the light inside is nonexistent, and yet I love it. I know lots of people are looking forward to next year’s venue at the Portland Convention Center, but I’m going to miss the dingy, dark industrial setting at the boatyard. It has its charm, even if you might trip in a pothole while sweating out every pore of your body while trying to enjoy said charm.

Bespoke Dresden has the opposite venue: the second and third floor of a skylight-filled German airport.

I think most of my photos from the event were shot at ISOs below 800, a pleasant change. Photographing bikes was harder; navigating multiple escalators, stairs, or an elevator adds significant time. I only photographed 14 bikes at Bespoked while I shot 27 at Made. John had his workflow dialed in Dresden and shot more than he did at Made, which was crazy impressive. I really enjoyed the airy venue; it still had the industrial vibes I like, but in a clean, refined way.

Techno Culture

Another thing that I knew about going in but wasn’t sure what to think of was the displays. I once came across an Instagram Reel that explained why Germany gravitates towards electronic music, and I think it’s a rather fitting analogy for something that seems trivial: the displays at Bespoked.

In this video, the presenter explains that German society scores highly on uncertainty avoidance, the cultural preference for structure over chaos. Perhaps this is a symptom of the notoriously rigid societal expectations and German infrastructure, or the reason. There were two great examples of this on our train commutes in Germany. John got in trouble with the ticket lady for incorrectly stamping his train ticket, and a glass breaker intended for emergencies was captioned with “misuse will be punished.”

Anyways, back to the Instagram reel. The video explains that this rigorous adherence to structure is what allows the mind to unplug in the right setting. That is reflected in German EDM culture. The beat of German techno is monotonous, and the expectations for entering a German club are strict. Black clothing, stickers over camera lenses, and strict expectations regarding personal conduct actually facilitate interpersonal connection. By stripping much of the performance and synchronizing everyone’s brain waves to the same beat, personality is laid bare, and you somehow find a semblance of camaraderie with a room full of sweaty strangers.

But how does that connect to Bespoked?

Bespoked Booths as Canvases

Bespoked provides every exhibitor with a large wooden display and accompanying lighting. My concern was that the individuality and vision of every builder wouldn’t be on display. For example, at Made, every builder or booth is responsible for their display. Some are great. Some are not so great. That ends up having a huge effect on how showgoers interact with the booth and the bikes.

The most stunning bike might be on display in a pretty poorly curated display, and therefore, receive very little attention. Builders with a fine eye for design beyond bikes are rewarded, but novices are left shrouded in shadow. Bespoked fixed this issue. Every booth starts with the same canvas: a wooden board that is customized with peg boards and shelves. Integrated lighting becomes a constant, not a variable. By creating a strict outline and level playing field, ironically, the individuality of every builder flourished.

Now, the wares of every maker, be it bikes, bags, or components, were the display, not the booth itself. Take, for example, Jergen Gertze of Giawasa. It was his first show. The track bike he brought, Katana, was stunning. His display would not indicate that this was the first full-size bicycle that he had ever built, and I think that can only help new builders like him. This choice had the complete opposite effect that was anticipated.

Innovative Showcase

Seeing as we posted a rather controversial Dust Up on Europe being the new home of innovative bike design, I want to carefully and briefly touch on that. When I say brief, I mean brief. I’m going to give you one, maybe two, perhaps three paragraphs on the subject.

After walking around the venue for only 30 minutes, I told John just how different I thought the bikes were. There were certainly lots of funky bikes designed to be just that, contraptions for the sake of enjoyment at a bike show, but there were also innovative bikes meant to be just as functional as they were eye-catching.

The pervasive bike culture in the United States is that bikes are toys first and tools second. In Europe, bikes as playthings certainly exist, but so do thousands of unassuming and uninteresting, everyday bikes locked up outside a train station, even in a smaller East German city not known for its bike infrastructure.

Good luck finding that in the US. I’m not here to debate why this is or to throw shade at anything. I just want to say that this mindset seems to be reflected in the types of bikes that framebuilders are making. I don’t have statistics or facts to back this up, just my overall impression.

Sport Versus Transport

The bikes at American shows tend to be far more expensive and far more focused on hobbies: racing, mountain biking, gravel biking, that sort of thing. In this European show, it felt like there were more bikes meant to be ridden every day and were priced more appropriately for such a life.

There were more “commuter bikes” like cargo bikes compared to “play bikes” like gravel bikes at Bespoked than at any other bike show I had attended. I don’t think there is anything better or worse about this difference; it is merely an observation. This is, after all, a written impression of a European bike show by a young American journalist who doesn’t yet own a cargo bike.

When I came back from Germany, friends asked me if I had fun or got to see much of Dresden and Germany. The reality of these events is that just about every waking hour is spent commuting to and from the venue, taking photos, walking bikes between booths and photo spots, editing, writing, or engaging in the dinner pleasantries associated with the event.

European Impressions

Aside from the short bike ride I did aboard Petor’s “Room on the Broom” Drust or the one night of Technoclubbing, I did not get out much. And yet, I came back from Europe with a full heart. I met so many wonderful people at this show, and that alone made the short sleeps and long days worth it. I didn’t have to travel and see parts of the European continent that I haven’t in order to make this trip feel fulfilling.

Thank you to every single one of you who sent us an email, a DM, or a heartfelt hug at the event for being such a bright light.

I’m not quite sure how to wrap up this piece besides acknowledging that I don’t think it will be the last reflection I write about this event. I would love to have the opportunity to visit all of the Bespoked events, as I think they truly are something special.

Petor, and to all the others who help organize and put on these events, thank you for your work and dedication. To the builders and exhibitors, I can’t wait to see what the future has in store for you. Thank you, everyone.
